title: Whose work and everyday lives appear in art?
essentialQuestion: Whose work and everyday lives appear in art?
learningGoal: Explain how art can make work and everyday life its main subject, connect a work's subject with its patron and audience, and compare two works without treating either as a complete picture of society.

evidence.question: The southern Low Countries, including present-day Belgium, in 1565, and rural France in 1855: different markets and audiences within Europe. Look at the whole of each work first, then at the people working in it.

sections.heading: Everyday work can become a major subject
sections.text:
Art does not show only rulers, famous events or extraordinary people. Artists have also pictured farming, preparing food, caring for others, travel and rest. These subjects make ordinary labour, or work done by people, visible. The ways that artworks were commissioned, sold and displayed also connect their subjects with the people who could afford to own them.

You saw The Harvesters in Lesson 1. Pieter Bruegel the Elder painted it in 1565, and he arranged workers across a landscape. Some gather grain; others eat or rest under a tree. The Met's family guide connects the picture with the traditional theme of work through the seasons. Distant houses, a church and boats place the harvest within a larger world where people live. The labour of producing food and everyday life share the same scene.
sections.simpler:
Art does not show only kings and famous events. Artists also painted farming, cooking, caring, travel and rest. These pictures make labour easy to see. Labour is work done by people. How a work was sold also matters. It links the picture with the people rich enough to own it.

You saw The Harvesters in Lesson 1. Bruegel painted it in 1565. Workers spread across the land. Some cut grain. Others eat or rest under a tree. A museum guide links it with the work of each season. Far away are houses, a church and boats. So the harvest is part of a bigger world. Labour and daily life share one scene.

sections.heading: A merchant's picture of farm work
sections.text:
The Met's collection record says that an Antwerp merchant commissioned the painting for his country house. He was its patron, the person who paid for it. The museum describes the workers as shown with sympathy, but idealised: presented as more orderly and perfect than real life. The painting's first owner and the farm workers in it had very different places in society. Its ordered plenty is one way of presenting rural life, not a complete record of it.

Bruegel's setting belongs to the southern Low Countries, including land that is now in Belgium. Antwerp was a major port and art market. The Met describes how trade and cultural contacts attracted artists and supported workshops. They also encouraged artists to make works for buyers beyond one town. A picture of the countryside could therefore belong to a business world in the city. This is context for the commission. It does not mean that every farmer shared the merchant's wealth, or that one painting represents all European life.
sections.simpler:
The museum says a trader in Antwerp paid for the painting. He was its patron. A patron pays for a work. It hung in his country house. The museum says the workers are shown kindly. But they are idealised. That means they look neater and better than in real life. The rich owner and the farm workers had very different lives. So the painting shows one view of farm life, not all of it.

Antwerp was in the southern Low Countries. Today that land is in Belgium. Antwerp was a busy port. Art was bought and sold there. Artists came for work. They made art for buyers in many towns. So a picture of farm work could belong to a rich city world. This does not mean every farmer was rich. And one painting does not show all of Europe.

sections.heading: A print for new buyers
sections.text:
Almost three centuries later, Jean-François Millet made an etching called The Gleaners. An etching is a print made from a prepared metal plate. The National Gallery of Art's example dates to 1855. Three figures bend to gather crops left over after the harvest. This lesson uses the print, not Millet's better-known oil painting of a related subject from 1857. Fine lines, repeated poses and the way the figures sit in the field organise the viewer's attention.

The Nelson-Atkins Museum holds another example of the etching and explains its market. Millet began making prints in the mid-1850s, partly to earn money and to reach possible buyers. Pictures of the countryside appealed to middle-class ideas about the dignity of work. Such calm, reassuring pictures could exist alongside fears of social conflict after the upheavals of 1848. What an artwork shows and why its audience valued it are not always the same.

These examples connect art with food, labour, class and the market for pictures. A wealthy buyer could admire a picture of work without sharing the worker's life. An artist could make workers important while also needing buyers. Neither relationship automatically makes the art dishonest. It makes production and ownership part of its history. Dates, materials, patrons and markets help explain why pictures of ordinary labour belonged in collections as well as in the fields they showed.
sections.simpler:
Almost 300 years later, Millet made The Gleaners. It is an etching. An etching is a print made from a metal plate. This one is from 1855. Three people bend down. They pick up crops left after the harvest. This is the print, not his famous painting from 1857. Thin lines and the same bent shapes guide our eyes.

Another museum has a copy of this etching. It says Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints helped him find buyers. Many buyers were middle class. They liked the idea that farm work was good and honest. These calm pictures sold at a time of fear. People worried about conflict after the troubles of 1848. So why people liked a picture can differ from what it shows.

A rich buyer could like a picture of work without doing that work. An artist could show workers with respect and still need buyers. That does not make the art false. It means making and owning art are part of its story. Dates, materials, patrons and buyers all help explain these pictures of labour.

glossary.definition: Work done by people, often with their hands.
glossary.example: The Harvesters shows the labour of cutting grain.

glossary.definition: A person or group who pays for or orders an artwork.
glossary.example: The patron of The Harvesters was a merchant from Antwerp.

glossary.definition: Showing something as neater or more perfect than it really is.
glossary.example: The museum calls the workers in the painting idealised.

glossary.definition: A print made from a metal plate that has lines cut into it.
glossary.example: Millet's The Gleaners is an etching, not a painting.

write.prompt: Explain how the market for Millet's prints connects a picture of farm work with buyers in towns and cities. Two or three sentences are enough.
sentenceStarters: So a picture of farm work ...
write.example: Millet made prints partly to earn money. Prints also helped him reach new buyers. Many of his buyers were middle-class people, not farm workers. They liked pictures of the countryside because of their own ideas about the dignity of work. So The Gleaners shows three people bending in a field. But it was made to be sold to people whose lives were very different from theirs.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, compare one choice Bruegel made in his painting with one choice Millet made in his print. Think about how many workers there are and how big they look.
speak.independentTask: Say or type a short comparison of one choice in the painting and one choice in the print.

prompts.text: One thing an image of work can show, and one thing it may leave out, is ...

reflect.completionMessage: You finished Lesson 12. You compared a painting and a print of farm work and saw how their buyers are part of their history.

sensitiveNotes: No learner is asked about their own or their family's work, income or class. Keep the discussion on the two works and their buyers.
educatorNotes: An image that is sympathetic to workers is not necessarily an unfiltered record of their conditions. Both works are chosen views made for buyers; neither is a social survey.

Answer points for Write: prints gave Millet income and reached buyers; middle-class audiences could value pictures of rural labour for reasons shaped by their own position. Accept a supported explanation without assuming every viewer thought alike.

This is Millet's etching of 1855 (the National Gallery of Art's impression), not his better-known oil painting of 1857. The Nelson-Atkins label, used for the market for his prints, describes another impression of the etching, which it dates 1855–56; keep the National Gallery of Art's 1855 date for the pictured impression.

Antwerp's port economy, mobile artists and art market come from The Met's essay Northern Mannerism in the Early Sixteenth Century. Bruegel's painting is later than that essay's main examples and is not being assigned to their style. The seasonal theme and the wider landscape come from The Met's family guide.
The first picture is the same file as Lesson 1's second picture (The Met's photograph of The Harvesters), reused and labelled as a revisit; it is not a second object.
The National Gallery of Art's record spells the French title “Les Glanenses”; the usual French is “Les Glaneuses”, used here.
